transcript.content: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Well, what brings me in is that I just keep getting stuck on this sagging, uneven look around my jaw and one side of my face. It really started bothering me after I saw myself in a bunch of recent family photos. I just can't seem to stop focusing on it, even though my wife and my clients at work say they barely notice anything at all. It's just... hard for me to ignore.
Do you find yourself repeatedly checking your reflection in mirrors or other surfaces throughout the day?

Yeah, I do. Especially before I sit down with a client. I’ll usually go check the bathroom mirror, or just pull out my phone camera a few times. I find myself adjusting the lighting, or maybe changing how my collar sits, just trying to find a better angle for my face. 

And then... I also notice I do a lot of comparing. Like, I'll be talking to the younger advisors at work, or people at gallery events, and I catch myself comparing my face to theirs instead of actually focusing on the conversation.
Outside of your concerns about your appearance, do you experience repetitive, unwanted thoughts or routines about other things in your life?

No, not really. Um, it's pretty much just this issue with my face. I don't have any other routines or... thoughts that get stuck like that. I mean, I'm organized at work, but just the normal amount you'd expect. So, yeah, nothing else really bothers me that way.
Do you ever feel that your perception of your face might be exaggerated, or are you completely convinced that the defect is as severe as you see it?

I mean... I guess part of me knows it might not be as bad as I think it is. Like I said, my wife tells me she doesn't see it, and I know she wouldn't lie to me. But when I look in the mirror, it just... it looks really obvious to me. So, I don't know. I guess I'm not completely convinced it's a huge deformity, but it still feels really significant when I'm the one looking at it.

latest_inference.note: Ruled out F22 because the patient retains insight and recognizes that the perceived flaw may not be as severe as it feels, ruling out a fixed somatic delusion.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient demonstrates persistent preoccupation with a perceived physical defect or asymmetry in his jaw and face that is imperceptible or barely noticeable to others (dysmorphophobia/body dysmorphic disorder, classified under F45.2 in ICD-10). He engages in repetitive mirror checking, camouflaging/adjusting collar and lighting, and compulsive comparison with others. General obsessive-compulsive disorder (F42) is ruled out as obsessions and compulsions are strictly limited to bodily appearance.
